  `run:` is unchanged: it never suspends, and answers in the turn it's asked in, as `draw` and
  `kinds` do. Write the `runAsync:` label out: a trailing closure that doesn't await picks `run:`.
- **It may be cancelled.** `canvas` hanging up (its timeout, ^C) cancels the request's task,
  answered `cancelled`, which nobody reads; closing its file answers it `board_closed` ("The board
  was closed before the command finished.") at once, and cancels it. What a cancelled command
  returns later is dropped, so a long wait looks at `Task.isCancelled` (a query does every 256
  shapes and before every slice; a model's call is cancelled at once). Every command, `draw`
  included, runs one main-actor hop after its request, so one cancelled, or whose file closed, before
  it starts never runs.
- **`canvas` waits as long as its params say**: the longest `x-timeout` among those given (`--ask`'s
  60 s), else 10 s, unless `--timeout` says ([above](#the-command-line)). The protocol stays 2: a
  param's `x-timeout`, and an error's `column` and `length`, are what an older `canvas` passes over
  (it waits 10 s, and says `timed_out`). `Registry.runAutomationCommand(_:params:editor:)` and
  `ShippedPlugins.commands(in:)` are async, and a test awaits them with TestKit's `awaitResult`.

### draw

`draw` is how an agent puts things on a board. It reads a script in a small language whose idea is
[reladraw](https://github.com/reladraw/reladraw)'s (Apache-2.0; the attribution is in
[THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md), and the language isn't called that): each
line says what a shape is, what it's called and where it sits against shapes already named, never
at coordinates, and the app works out only the distances.

```
sticky-note "Web" text: "Browser app"
sticky-note "API" right of "Web" text: "Public HTTP API"
subboard "Payments" below "API"
edge "Web" -> "API"
```

A shape's title is its name. A statement about a title the board has changes that shape (only what
it says, and it moves only with a placement), and one about a title it doesn't makes a new one. A
gap is a minimum among the shapes the script places; shapes already on the board stay put, and
are kept clear of; and whatever is ambiguous (an axis nothing settles, two shapes with nothing to
hang on, two that would overlap with nothing saying which side either sits on) is refused rather
than guessed. A placement is worked out once: the board keeps positions, never `right of "API"`.
The language itself, every construct and every refusal, is written for agents in the canvas skill
([`.claude/skills/canvas`](../.claude/skills/canvas/SKILL.md): `SKILL.md`, a tour, and
`reference/language.md`, the whole of it), and CompositionTests runs every example in it and
holds its tables of kinds to `canvas kinds`, so the skill can't drift from the app
([Testing plugins](#testing-plugins)).

How it's built ([Draw.swift](../Sources/Automation/Draw.swift) and the files beside it), in four
steps, the first three against the board as the run starts:

1. **Read.** DrawScript's `Script(parsing:)` cuts the script into statements, one a line: shapes
   (any first word but `edge`, `delete` and `style` is a kind word, left for Automation to
   resolve), edges (`from:`, `to:`, `via:` and `share:` are the language's own keys, `EdgeKey`; `via:`'s value
   is a kind word, found by Automation, and `share:`'s is `true` or a title, `EdgeShare`), deletes, and styles, which it merges into the statements that
   name them. An attribute that isn't the language's own is a key and a value, left for Automation to
   check against the kind. The language's own words are enums with implicit raw values (`Keyword`,
   `LanguageKey`, `EdgeKey`, `Direction`, …), never string literals, so the id audit never sees
   another module's id there (Connections' `channel`, Titles' `title`). Every line that can't be read is
   reported, up to 20.
2. **Resolve** (`Drawing`): each kind word against the registry (a kind is drawable when a tool
   places it, `registry.placement(for:)`); each title, through DrawNames, to the one board shape it
   names (restated) or to none (made); each attribute by the kind's schema, own and added
   properties alike (`KindVocabulary`, over the core's [`KindSchema`](#a-kinds-schema): a value
   read as its property's type, in draw's own words when it can't be, and JSON held to the
   schema before it's read, `registry.schemaViolations(of:kind:)`, since reading drops a member its
   type doesn't have without a word: an unknown member, or a value of the wrong type anywhere in
   it, is `invalid_value`, with a "did you mean" over the object's members; a property the schema marks `readOnly` is no attribute (`unknown_attribute`; `kinds` leaves it out), and a string whose `format` is `x-canvas-query` is checked by `editor.queries?.check` (syntax and vocabulary, so a bad one is `invalid_value` with the engine's message and hint; unchecked without QueriesPlugin; Automation, a language, uses Queries, a surface), and a string whose `contentMediaType` is one a plugin
   writes (`DrawTextFormats`: mention text's) is written by that plugin, wherever it is in the value, `DrawTexts.swift`; the naming property and
   coordinates refused); each placement's targets; each edge's ends and attribute keys; and each
   delete's shape, with the connections on it (those DrawEdges' `ends` joins to it, and any other
   of the edge kind bound to it, `record.boundShapes(in:)`: one with an end left free) and the
   boards it owns (a subboard's, and every board under it, `file.subtree(ownedBy:)`: refused,
   `read_only`, if one holds a read-only shape, as a transaction would refuse the delete; else said
   in a warning). A new shape starts as what its tool places (`placement.shape(at:)`), and every
   shape's attributes are set by the core (`registry.shape(_:setting:)`), so the registry builds
   every record, and what the kind derives from them (a note's height, from its
   text, `DerivedProps`) is the size it's placed at, unless the statement gives one; given a width
   alone (`size: 300x`, a `Size` with no height), the shape is built at that width and what the
   kind derives is put in step there, whether any property is set or not (`registry.derived(_:)`),
   so a note is that wide and as tall as its text in one run, and a kind that derives nothing keeps
   its height; a `size:` under the smallest the kind's placement draws (`Placement.minimumSize`: a
   frame's 96 × 64, its tool's and resizing's too) is `invalid_value`, as one too big is, and `kinds`
   says it (`smallest`). What a shape is bound to
   (`ShapeReferencing`) must be on the board as the script leaves it, or it's `invalid_value`; what
   it only names (`ShapeNaming`, a note's mentions) needn't be. A kind whose titles are only
   derived (no shipped kind's) takes no title in its statement
   (`untitlable`), and a restated one whose derived title changes is renamed (`renamed`, held to a
   rename's rules), where one that's named too (no shipped kind is) keeps its derived title or is
   refused (`renames`). Problems that don't depend on one another are all reported, up to 20,
   each statement's first.
3. **Place** (DrawScript's `LayoutProblem.solve()`, from a problem built in DrawLayout.swift): the
   shapes that move are free boxes (new ones, and those restated with placements); what their
   placements name that stays put is fixed (board shapes, `board`, `view`); and every board shape
   with a solid that the script doesn't move or delete is an obstacle. What has a solid is the
   core's to say (`ShapeContext.solidBounds(of:)`: a shape's bounds where its geometry is closed,
   finite and not flat; none for an arrow or a line, or a shape kept aside), so a placement of any
   plugin keeps clear of the same shapes. The obstacles are filed once a run, in paint order, in a
   grid of cells about a shape's size (DrawScript's `ObstacleGrid`, boxes only, which Automation's
   `ObstacleIndex` fills in a pass over the board, keeping each obstacle's shape beside it), and the
   solver asks for them by region, each answer kept for the run: it asks again after every push,
   mostly about boxes that haven't moved, so however often it asks, a question costs what's near
   the box it's about (`./build.sh bench` holds a draw of 20 notes, each pushed along a row of the
   10,000-shape board to its end, to 150 ms). DrawScript knows only boxes: a part on an outline (a
   round shape's corner) is worked out by Automation from the shape's `ShapeGeometry`, and handed
   over as a rect. The solver's first problem is the one reported. A zone isn't in a box's way
   (`Solver.isZone`): an obstacle that wholly holds a
   restated box where it already sat, however snug; a shape the box is placed against, at twice
   that one's area; the box where it lands and another shape too, at twice the box's area, so a
   region that frames what's in it takes a legend in any corner of the view or the board on it;
   or the `view` the box is placed against, or its drawing with nothing to hang on is drawn in,
   whatever its size (that drawing's spot isn't kept clear of it). A shape held is a board shape,
   or a free box the zone counts (`Solver.counted(by:in:)`, once a solve for each zone asked
   about): one on it for a reason of its own, `inside` or `on` it, a zone for it without counting
   any free box, or placed against one that counts, worked out from those up until nothing is
   added, so two new shapes can't hold each other on an empty note. What holds only the box where
   it lands is a neighbor, and in the way: an empty note or card next door, or a lone shape that's
   the whole board, for a box inside `board` (a note holding a badge of its own is a container
   like any other). A box held where it lands wholly on such a region at twice its size is
   `unordered`, its hint saying what the region holds (nothing yet, or no shape wholly: one hangs
   over its edge) and offering first to place the box elsewhere, since the region may be a note
   whose words it would cover, then, if the region is meant to hold shapes, to place a first one
   inside it. With the boxes placed, it says which obstacles each sits on as zones
   (`LayoutSolution.zones`, never what it's `inside` or `on`), which it's raised above and warned
   about hanging over.
4. **Apply**, in one `editor.transact("Draw")` (DrawCommit.swift), one undo step, which says an
   agent made it (`transaction.byAgent`: a type's sync takes what it wrote as in step, and
   asks the model nothing): the deletes; the shapes, each after
   every script shape it's drawn inside or on, new or restated, so that shape is in place first
   (new ones inserted on top; restated ones updated in place, and raised above a shape they're
   moved inside or on, or a zone they sit in where they land, while they're writable: before a
   change that locks one, after one that unlocks it, and not at all for one read-only throughout,
   which placing left as it was); the edges, through DrawEdges, against `transaction.shapes`, so either
   end may be new, each one's channel and sides checked as it's made, the first that's wrong
   ending the run; then the result, read back from `transaction.document`, and the warnings. Anything wrong throws out of
   the body, and a body that throws commits nothing, and makes no undo step
   ([the document](#the-editor-the-document-and-drawing)).
   A dry run is the same transaction, whose body throws its finished result (a private error
   `draw` catches), so on the same board a dry run and a real run say the same.

**Containers** (a frame, [`ShapeContaining`](#containers)) are where the in-or-out rule meets the
language:

- **`in "X"`, for X a container**, draws on the board X is on and puts the shape in X: it's kept
  within X, 40 in from each side, as `inside` keeps a box (the layout problem's `Free.holder`,
  checked as `inside` is, `no_room` when it can't be), wherever its placements put it there; with
  none, and not in X already (where a restated shape stays), it's placed as `inside "X" top-left`
  places one, a clause written `in "X"`, so several make a list down from there. X must be on the
  board as the run starts (`unsupported` for one the script draws: draw it, then what's in it),
  writable (a read-only one, a locked frame, is `read_only`: nothing goes in it), and neither the
  shape nor one it holds (`circular`).
- **What a run puts down settles as by hand**, one by one, once every shape is where it goes, so
  each is judged against where the others land, never where a shape the run moves was
  (`transaction.settle`; the shapes that hold none first, then the containers, so what's put down
  in one goes along if it's nudged): a new shape, and a restated one it places or resizes, over a
  container's edge goes wholly in or
  out by most of its area, nudged, said in a warning (`"N" was over the edge of "Pen", so it was
  nudged in`), and glided after a real run (`editor.glide`); a container put down takes in what it
  lands on, and what it holds over its new edge goes in or out, said too (`a shape over the edge of
  "Pen" was nudged wholly in or out of it`); a read-only container it would go into refuses the
  run (`read_only`). So `inside`, `on` and landing on a zone put a shape in a container too, and a
  container's edge is never a zone's to warn about.
- **A restated container placed elsewhere takes what it holds along** (`translate`), which is
  never in its way (`Free.carries`), and which every other shape the run places meets where the
  container takes it, never where it is now: kept clear of it there, as of a part of the
  container (a shape `in` the container is; one placed over where it was isn't), so containers
  can trade places in one run. A placement against what it takes along is `unsupported`, since
  the layout has that where it was. Containers are applied before what they hold.
- **Read-only is inherited** (`transaction.isReadOnly(_:)` and `BoardReading.isReadOnly(_:)`, which
  read a shape through the board it's on): a shape in a locked frame, or on a locked subboard's
  board, refuses a real change and a delete (`read_only`), as a locked shape does.
- **A board that can't change takes nothing new**: a locked subboard's board, and every board under
  it (`reading.isBoardReadOnly`). `in` the subboard is `read_only` as `in` a locked frame is
  (`"Plans" is read-only (locked, say), so nothing goes in it`, the same hint), and so is a new
  shape that would land there by its placements or by the board shown (`"N" would go on "Plans"'s
  board, which is read-only (locked, say)`, named as `several_boards` names a board, by the shape
  that holds it), and a new edge (`edge "A" -> "B" would go on …`), the first thing wrong with each
  statement in a script, found as the run starts, or, for an edge, as it's applied; nothing is
  drawn, a dry run says the same, and no step is made. A restatement that changes nothing still
  goes through (`unchanged`).
- **`delete` of a container** leaves what it holds where it is, now in what held the container
  (the core's), a locked shape too, and says nothing more.

**Edges through a stand-in** ([DrawStandIns.swift](../Sources/Automation/DrawStandIns.swift),
[DrawBoard.swift](../Sources/Automation/DrawBoard.swift)). An arrow can't leave its board, and a
shape that many arrows point at needn't be pointed at from everywhere, so an edge may go into a
[stand-in](#stand-ins-forwarding) for one end, put beside the other. Automation knows no kind of
stand-in and nothing of publicness: it asks `registry.standIns` which kinds stand in, which of them
can be made to stand for a shape (`makers`) and which shapes each admits (Topology's
[`makes` and `needs`](#stand-ins-forwarding)), and References' `reference` is what answers.

- **Whether.** A statement says so with `via: <kind>`: a kind word that must be one of `makers`
  (else `invalid_value`, with the one it's like and the kinds there are) and admit the end it stands
  for (else `invalid_value`, saying what the kind `needs`: "only a public shape can be stood for", and
  to ask the user, since `public:` is theirs to set and a script never makes a shape public to get an
  edge across). Otherwise **`Drawing.goesThroughStandIn(from:to:)` decides, the one function that
  does**, and the place to grow: today an edge goes through a stand-in when its ends are on different
  boards, and nothing else decides (a rule about distance or kinds would go there, and nowhere else).
  It goes through the first of `makers` that admits the end stood for (`standInKind(for:)`), and only
  the edge's row says so (`via`), as where `via:` asked: a warning for each edge between boards would
  bury the warnings that need reading in a run of many. Where no kind admits it, the edge is `several_boards`, with a hint that only such a shape can be stood for and to
  ask the user (`Drawing.standInHint`); where nothing stands in at all, the hint is the old one.
- **Sharing** (`share: true`, `share: "A"`; `sharedStandIn`). Each edge through a stand-in makes one of
  its own, so a hub with many users has as many, and `share:` makes them one. `share: true` draws the
  arrow into a direct stand-in of the kind for the same end that is already in the innermost container
  of the end that stays (the frame it is in, or the board outside frames: `containerOfEnd`), the
  board's first in document order (found in one pass, `boardStandIns(for:)`, deleted ones left out)
  or one an earlier edge of the run made (`madeStandIns`); with none, it makes one, as without.
  `share: "A"` takes the one A's own arrow goes into, A (a shape of the script or the board) being in
  that container, from A's edges above it in the script and then the board's (`connected(to:)`), and
  never makes one: A with none is `invalid_value`, naming A and the end, and so is A in another
  container, or the edge's own end. On an edge that goes through none (both ends on the board, no
  `via:`) it is `invalid_value` too, unless the edge is drawn through a stand-in already. The row of
  an edge that reused one says `shared: true` and `sharedWith` (the title named); an edge drawn
  already says `unchanged` with the same flags, `shared` then meaning that an arrow from another
  shape runs to the same stand-in (`Connected.shared`, `sharing(of:match:among:)`). Nothing else
  changes: a shared stand-in is deleted like any, once no arrow is on it.
- **Which end.** The one off the board the run draws on; with `via:`, the arrow's end (however the
  edge is written, `<-` too), put beside the start. Either end may be the far one: a stand-in for the
  start, the arrow running out of it.
- **The board** (`Drawing.board(for:in:)`, `DrawBoard.swift`; `BoardClaims` reads the statements).
  An edge between shapes on two boards claims a board only softly with an end some stand-in can be
  made for (`makers`, `admits`) and hard with one that can't; the run draws on the first hard claim,
  else on the board of the first such edge's start (`via:`'s start claims hard, since the stand-in is
  put beside it), and each such edge needs one end on it (`several_boards` otherwise, naming the end
  it can't reach). `delete edge` claims the same way. Two edges claim otherwise:
  - One that's **drawn through a stand-in already** (an arrow on one of its two boards between the
    end there and a direct stand-in for exactly the other, by `edgeMatches`, the one rule for which
    arrows are an edge, whichever board it's asked of) claims that board, the start's first, hard,
    and its other end claims nothing, whether or not that end can be stood for still. The run draws
    where the stand-in is, so a run again, a `via:` over it and a `delete edge` find the edge there,
    rather than make a second stand-in for it on the other board. Each board's arrows are read once
    a run, and only for an edge between boards (`AutomationPlugin.boardConnectionsRead`, debug
    builds, counts them).
  - One that joins **a shape the script draws** (a title no board has: it's on the board the run
    draws on, whichever that is) to a shape the file has: the script's end claims nothing, and the
    file's claims as an end of an edge between boards does, softly if a stand-in can be made for it
    (with nothing else to say, the run goes to its board, and the edge is straight there), else hard
    (and the hint asks for it to be made so, as it does for any end).

  A script with no edge between boards reads none of this (a board's arrows are read only when one
  shows up). `Drawing` reads `standIns` for a script with any edge or delete: a delete's arrows may
  run into stand-ins.
- **The stand-in is a shape of the run.** `registry.standIns.make` makes the record (the kind's
  tool's shape, standing for the end, called as the end's title folds), and `routeEdge` adds it to
  the run as a `ShapeItem` (`standsFor` set), placed as any new shape is: right of the start where
  that's the end that stays, left of the end where that is, or on the side `from:` or `to:` names for
  the end that stays, at the normal gap, kept clear of what's there, and settled into the containers
  it lands on. It has no placement of the script's, so where it clashes with another free box that
  nothing orders it against (two stand-ins beside notes side by side) it's the one that moves,
  past the other, on the axis its own placements leave free (`LayoutProblem.Free.implied`,
  `Solver.yielding`), where a box the script wrote would be `unordered`; its push warns, naming `from:`
  and `to:` as the fix. The stand-ins beside one shape on one side are a list of their own, 16
  apart (`LayoutProblem.impliedListStep`: a pill has no title above it to leave room for), never with
  a shape the script places there, which stays where its placement puts it while they give way past
  it (`Solver.findLists` keys implied boxes apart, and lists by what placements say, not their
  text). A list moves as one, down the page or across (`Solver.listHolds`, each member held where the
  first solve puts it from the one before), and is as free to move as all its members are, so a push
  never splits a column. Beside a shape the run doesn't move, a stand-in joins the column a run
  before left on that side (`Drawing.columnEnd`: of the stand-ins an arrow joins to it, those wholly
  that side of it, in line as a list lines them, on the nearest line whose stand-ins reach across from
  its middle, so one dragged off elsewhere isn't beside it), 16 past its end
  and in line with it, its placements said in words (`Clause.written(_:naming:gap:)`), rather than
  centered on the shape and pushed past the column. It's inserted before the arrow, in the run's one
  transaction.
- **Its channel and sides** are the edge maker's: `EdgeRequest.fromStandsFor` and `toStandsFor` say
  the kinds of what an end stands for (none for a shape itself), and `PortEdgesPlugin` judges the end
  as those kinds would be, on the stand-in's own sides
  ([below](#edges-and-their-channels-portedgesplugin)).
- **Matching**, for a run again and for `delete edge` (`edgeMatches`): an arrow between one end and a
  stand-in whose record stands for exactly the other, by `.shapes` (a `.provided` answer can change,
  so it never matches), is the edge, straight or through, on one board too without `via:`; the
  stand-in the edge would make is then skipped, so a run again makes none. An arrow through a
  stand-in is looked for before anything else is decided about the edge (`routeEdge`), so it's the
  edge whatever the shape it stands for can be stood for now (it may have stopped being public), with
  `via:` or without; one drawn straight is looked for after `via:` is checked against the end. `via:`
  written over an edge drawn straight, or through a stand-in for its start, is `invalid_value` (`the
  edge "A" -> "B" is drawn straight to "B"`), the hint saying to `delete edge` it above the line; two
  matches are `ambiguous_edge`, as two straight ones are.
- **Deletes.** `delete edge` takes what matches, either way round for `<->`, and `delete "X"` every
  connection bound to X; then each stand-in at the other end of one (a direct one, as matching reads
  them, never one whose answer can change) that the run leaves with no arrow at all, loose ones
  included, goes too (`standInsEmptied`): it has no title for a script to name, and it stood for its
  shape for those arrows alone. One that's read-only is `read_only` (`the reference that delete "X"
  leaves with no arrow is read-only (locked, say)`), and nothing is deleted. A stand-in for X with
  arrows from elsewhere stays, which is what a stand-in several edges share does until the last of them goes.
- **The result.** An edge's row has `via` (the stand-in's kind) whenever its arrow goes through one,
  `unchanged` and `deleted` rows too (a `delete "X"`'s among them, naming the shape a stand-in stands
  for, as an edge's row does); the stand-in has a row of its own on its statement's line: `created`,
  with its `kind` and `at` and no title, before the edge's; `deleted`, with its kind alone, after its
  arrows'. A dry run says the same, and one undo takes the stand-in and the arrow back together.

Before any of it, a run is refused while a drag is under way on the board (`editor.session`,
`busy`: its Escape would put back what the script moved), or a press is held
(`undoHistory.isPressHeld`: whatever commits during a press is part of its undo step, so the run
would be taken back with it). Once it's placed, a
real run ends an edit under way on a shape it changes or deletes (`editor.endEditing()`), and works
the script out again if ending it changed the board, so what's typed lands first. It applies the
run once and throws it away before it does, since some of what a run can fail on (an edge that
can't be drawn) is found only as it's applied: a run that fails, or leaves that shape as it is,
leaves the typing be. The view the script's `view` and its unplaced drawing go by is where the
camera is headed (`editor.cameraTarget`), so a draw just after a `--reveal` goes where that one's
glide ends. The selection is left alone, and so is the camera,
unless `--reveal` asks to ease it to fit what the run made or changed
(`editor.animateCamera(to: Camera(fitting:…))`, as selecting a row of the table of contents does).

What comes back (`DrawResult`, with the server's `board`) says what each statement did, in line
order, and never by id, since titles are the names:

```json
{"board": {"id": 2, "name": "Architecture", "shows": "root", "showsPath": ["root"]},
 "changes": [{"line": 2, "did": "created", "kind": "sticky-note", "title": "API", "at": [[620, 350], [200, 200]], "inView": true},
             {"line": 4, "did": "connected", "kind": "arrow", "from": "Web", "to": "API", "channel": "note-link"}, …],
 "warnings": [{"line": 3, "message": "\"Ship v1\": Blocked: say why in the notes.", "severity": "warning", "attribute": "notes"}]}
```

A row's `did` is `created`, `moved` (its bounds changed), `updated`, `renamed` (with `was`),
`unchanged`, `deleted`, `connected` or `reconnected`. A shape's row has its `kind`, `title` and
`at` (`[[x, y], [width, height]]`, world units), `inView` while the board is in a window, and
`pushedPast`; an edge's has `from`, `to`, `via` where it goes through a stand-in, and the attributes
DrawEdges declares (`channel`; not its kind's, which are as written), but a
deleted connection with an end left free has neither end to name. A
warning (`line`, but none for one about the whole run; `message`; `severity`; and the property
it's about, `attribute`) is an issue DrawChecks finds on a shape made or changed (an `error`
too: the shape is drawn, invalid; without DrawChecks, a bound of its schema it breaks), a push
past another shape (or a move along with a shape pushed, which isn't in `pushedPast`: that's
only what the shape was kept clear of itself; what a shape went past is said once each way it
went, so a list's members, pushed past a wall in turn, aren't also said to have gone along with
one another past it), a named side facing away from the
other end, a new title nearly one the board has, a shape hanging over the edge of a zone it
sits in (a zone isn't in its way, but doesn't keep it in), how many shapes
landed out of view, a shape resized where it stays that now overlaps another, a name a shape
drawn holds (a mention in its text) of a shape that isn't in the file or is on a board the app
can't show (by id, since the script wrote it: `"Plan": text names shapes that aren't in the file:
…; they show as missing`), or a deleted subboard's boards and what was on them. A dry run's
result says `dryRun: true`. The result's `board` is the server's: the board the run worked on,
read as it began.

### measure

`canvas measure <script>|-` is for a tool that lays shapes out before it draws them, and needs what
only the app knows: the size `draw` would make each shape of a script (a note as tall as its text at
its width, a note that is a type as tall as its text), how far its title row reaches above it, how wide
a reference to a shape is for its title, and the constants placement is done with. It is an app
command (no `--board`), [Measure.swift](../Sources/Automation/Measure.swift): it reads the script as
`draw` does (the same messages), leaves out every placement, `in`, edge without `via:` and delete, and
runs the shape statements through `Drawing` itself on a board of its own, made empty and thrown away
(`CanvasEditor(registry:)`), so it reads no board of the file, changes none and opens no undo step, and
the sizes are the ones a draw makes (`Drawing.complete`, then `registry.derived`). It answers

```json
{"shapes": [{"line": 1, "title": "Checkout v2", "kind": "sticky-note", "size": [300, 200], "above": 27}],
 "references": [{"line": 4, "for": "Hub", "size": [91, 32]}],
 "constants": {"gaps": {"none": 0, "tight": 40, "normal": 80, "wide": 160}, "defaultGap": 80, "listStep": 64,
               "referenceStep": 16, "horizontalClearance": 40, "verticalClearance": 64, "frameInset": 40,
               "smallest": {"frame": [96, 64]}}}
```

`above` is `editor.adornmentExtent(of:)` (Adornments, which Automation may use as a surface): how far
the adornments the shape would show reach above its top edge at 100% zoom, where they keep their size
in view points (`AdornmentLayout.extent(of:in:)`, pure over the layout, so text left out for want of
room reaches nowhere); asked of a record that is not on any board, nothing is kept for it. A reference
row is the size of `registry.standIns.make(kind, standingFor:, label:)` for the end's title, for each
edge that says `via:` (the kind it names): Automation knows no kind of stand-in, and a bare edge's goes
through one or not by the boards, which it does not read. The constants are read from the source and
never copied: the gaps (`GapName`), the step between references (`LayoutProblem.impliedListStep`), the
inset of what `in "F"` holds (`LayoutProblem.insideGap`), the default gap, the list step, the
clearances, and each kind's least size (`Placement.minimumSize`).

### What draw takes from other plugins

Automation knows no title, port, validity or mention. `draw` takes each from a point Automation declares
([DrawPoints.swift](../Sources/Automation/DrawPoints.swift)), keyed so it takes at most one
contribution (one for each media type, for text), which DrawLexicon makes, a plugin value for each
concern it imports (AutomationTests make their own, over fixtures). Without one, `draw` does without:

| Point | Sugar | What `draw` gets | Without it | Shipped |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `DrawNames` | `registrar.drawNames(name:namingProperty:isDerived:fold:)` | What a shape is called; the property of its kind's schema a title is written to (nil: its shapes can't be named); whether the kind works names out itself; how a title a script writes is folded | No titles: a titled statement is `no_names` | TitleNamesPlugin |
| `DrawEdges` | `registrar.drawEdges(kind:attributes:sides:ends:make:)` | The kind edges are (nil while nothing makes them); the attribute keys an edge takes beside `from:` and `to:`; what an edge may leave a kind on, by side (for `kinds`); which shapes a connection joins; a connection made or changed | No edges: an edge statement is `no_edges` | PortEdgesPlugin |
| `DrawChecks` | `registrar.drawChecks { record, shapes in … }` | What's wrong with a shape made or changed, as the script leaves the board: `DrawIssue`s (a message, whether it's an error, the property it's about) | Each shape checked against its kind's schema (`registry.schemaViolations(of:)`) | ValidationChecksPlugin |
| `DrawTextFormats` | `registrar.drawTextFormat(mediaType:describes:write:)` | Each string a script writes whose schema says `contentMediaType` of that media type, as `write` gets it (its string's escapes undone) with a `DrawTextContext` (the registry, the string's schema as its kind declares it, and `shape(called:admitting:)`, which finds the shape a title names as the script finds one, `admitting` taking the record and the keys the script writes on it, for a shape drawn in the same run: what to keep, or a refusal. `describes` is said after the attribute's type in `canvas kinds`. A list whose schema is `uniqueItems` is written with each once, the first, after its strings are written (two titles of one shape are one id) | Text kept as written; `kinds` says nothing after its type | MentionTextsPlugin, TypeNamesPlugin |

`TypeNamesPlugin` ([TypeNames.swift](../Sources/DrawLexicon/TypeNames.swift)) writes `is: "Employee card"`, on a shape and on an edge, as the id of the type that title names (`TypeLink.mediaType`), admitting what `TypeIndex.canBeNamed(_:registry:writing:)` says, a pure function of the record and the registry (a type; the custom shapes join it), and refuses any other shape "which isn't a type or a shape", and the shape itself (`DrawTextContext.owner`); a quoted value for a list of text is a list of that one item (Automation's, `KindVocabulary.value(of:)`), several are JSON.

DrawLexicon's four registrations, whole but for `PortEdgesPlugin`'s policy and the clauses `MentionTextsPlugin` says
([TitleNames.swift](../Sources/DrawLexicon/TitleNames.swift),
[PortEdges.swift](../Sources/DrawLexicon/PortEdges.swift), [ValidationChecks.swift](../Sources/DrawLexicon/ValidationChecks.swift),
[MentionTexts.swift](../Sources/DrawLexicon/MentionTexts.swift)):

```swift
// TitleNamesPlugin: a shape is called what Titles calls it, and a title is written to the one Titles keeps.
registrar.drawNames(name: { record, registry in registry.title(of: record) },
                    namingProperty: { kind, registry in
                        registry.properties(for: kind).contains(TitleProperty.key) ? TitleProperty.key.rawValue : nil
                    },
                    isDerived: { kind, registry in registry.titleIsDerived(kind) },
                    fold: { TitleProperty.folded($0) })

// PortEdgesPlugin: an edge is the connector's connection, on the channel this plugin picks.
registrar.drawEdges(kind: { registry in registry.makesConnections ? registry.connectorKind : nil },
                    attributes: [ChannelProperty.key.rawValue],
                    sides: { kind, registry in EdgeChannels.sides(of: kind, in: registry) },
                    ends: { record, registry in registry.connectionEnds(of: record) },
                    make: { request, existing, shapes throws(AutomationError) in
                        try EdgeChannels.connection(for: request, existing: existing, in: shapes)
                    })

// ValidationChecksPlugin: what's wrong is what Validation finds, schema bounds included.
registrar.drawChecks { record, shapes in
    shapes.registry.validationIssues(of: record, in: shapes).map { issue in
        DrawIssue(issue.message, isError: issue.severity == .error, field: issue.field)
    }
}

// MentionTextsPlugin: in mention text, `@[Title]` is the whole mention of the shape called Title.
registrar.drawTextFormat(mediaType: MentionTextFormat.mediaType, describes: "@[Title] mentions") { text, context throws(AutomationError) in
    let scope = context.schema[MentionTextFormat.annotationKey]?.objectValue
    return try MentionTextFormat.resolvingNames(in: text) { name throws(AutomationError) in
        let shape = try context.shape(called: name) { record in clause(context.registry.mentionAdmission(of: record, scope: scope)) }
        return (shape.id, shape.title)
    }
}
```

- **Names are titles.** A kind is named when it opts into the title Titles keeps (`title()`, or
  `registrar.title(K.self)` for another plugin's kind), derived when Titles works its titles out (`title { … }`),
  and may be both (no shipped kind is): a derived name names a shape only while it's the only one
  so called, and a statement that would change it is refused (`renames`). The
  board's names are read once a run, from the shapes that aren't kept aside. None of DrawLexicon's
  plugins writes another module's id: `TitleNamesPlugin` reaches `title` through
  `TitleProperty.key`, and `PortEdgesPlugin` `channel` through `ChannelProperty.key`.
- **An edge statement is an upsert.** `ends`, over the transaction's document, finds the
  connections already drawn from one shape to the other (either way round for `<->`; one drawn the
  other way round is asked for its own way). None: `make` gets `existing` nil, and draws one
  (`connected`). One: `make` changes it, or hands back `existing` itself when nothing would change,
  which is how `draw` tells `unchanged` from `reconnected` (`==`). More is `ambiguous_edge`. `make`
  gets an `EdgeRequest`: its ends by id, the sides named (`EdgeRequest.Side`, Automation's own,
  since DrawLexicon imports Automation, not DrawScript), whether `<->` puts a head
  at its start too, the attributes it declares as written, its ends' names and the edge as
  written, for messages, and, for an end that's a [stand-in](#draw) the run
  put beside the shape it connects, the kinds of what it stands for (`fromStandsFor`, `toStandsFor`:
  the end is judged as those shapes would be, on its own sides). It returns the connection, not inserted, and throws
  `AutomationError(message, reason:, hint:)`, which `draw` gives the statement's line; its closure
  says `throws(AutomationError)`, as a command's does. `draw` checks what comes back (the edge
  kind, a new id or the existing one, naming only shapes on the board) before it inserts or
  updates it. `DrawEdges.check` refuses an attribute key the language keeps (`from`, `to`, `via`,
  `style`), one a result's row has of its own (`line`, `did`, `kind`, …: a row carries an edge's
  attributes beside its own members), one a script couldn't write before a colon, and one declared
  twice.
- **An edge's other attributes are its kind's**, as a shape's are: any key DrawEdges doesn't
  declare is one of the edge kind's attributes (its schema's, read by `KindVocabulary`: an arrow's
  `text`, `labelPosition`, `bend`, `locked`), or `unknown_attribute`, read as a shape's value is.
  `make` never sees them: `draw` sets them on what it returns (`registry.shape(_:setting:)`), then
  hands that to `make` again as `existing`, and refuses one `make` changes back (`invalid_value`,
  "… isn't what the edge as written says": an arrow's heads are its arrow's, `->` or `<->`). So
  an edge restated without one keeps it, as a shape does, and DrawLexicon never learns what a kind says.
- **Checks see the board as the script leaves it** (`transaction.shapes`), so a rule that looks up
  another shape sees the ones drawn with it. Each issue is a warning on the statement's line.
- **A text is written by the format of its schema's media type** (`DrawTexts.swift`). `KindVocabulary`
  reads which of a kind's properties may hold such a string anywhere inside (`textKeys`: a `$ref`
  followed once, so a schema that holds itself ends), so a property that can't is passed over at
  once. A value that can (a string, a list, an object) is walked beside its property's schema,
  `properties`, `additionalProperties`, `prefixItems` and `items`, `$ref`s followed, members in
  name order so the first refusal is the same each time, and each string whose resolved schema
  says a media type some plugin writes goes through its `write`, as the script wrote it, with
  the string's schema as declared. It's after the value is read and held to its schema (`fits`), for
  a shape's attributes, a style's among them, and for an edge's own. A refusal is the statement's, said
  on its line as `"Plan": remark: …` (a shape's subject, the attribute, what the format said, and
  `(from style x)`), or `edge "A" -> "B": remark: …`, with the reason and hint it was thrown with;
  a title whose own statement couldn't be resolved adds no error of its own (`Drawing.skipped`, as a
  placement against it adds none). `canvas kinds` says what a format takes after the type of a property whose
  strings it writes (`KindVocabulary.compactType`: `text (@[Title] mentions)`, `JSON [text] (…)` for a list
  of them), so a refusal's hint says it too.
- **A format asks for a shape by title** (`DrawTextContext.shape(called:admitting:)`, `DrawTextLookup`),
  made once a run after every title the script draws is known, among the shapes `admitting` takes
  (a closure over the shape: nil takes it, a string says why it doesn't, as the clause that follows
  its kind). The places, in order, the first with a shape called that (folded as DrawNames folds)
  that is taken deciding: a shape the script draws, restates, or renames to it (`title: "New"`,
  known before the attributes are read, so a text earlier in the script finds it; the old title
  finds the same shape, as a placement does), also one drawn further down; the board the run draws
  on; the board the window shows (if another); then every other board of the file the app can
  show (the last two are `FileNames.beyond`, which finds an edge's end on another board too: the
  window's board if it has one, else the one other board that has one). Two or more in one place
  are `ambiguous_title` (those on the board by their kinds and where they are, as a placement's
  are; on other boards, by the boards); shapes the script deletes, and those on boards its
  deletes take, don't count, and a title only they have is `unknown_title` ("names "Old", which
  this script deletes"); a title some shape has and none is taken, `invalid_value`, saying
  what the first is and the format's clause; none at all, `unknown_title` with
  `Suggestions.closest` over the file's titles and the script's own that are taken. It
  never decides the board: `Drawing.board(for:in:)` reads statements' titles alone. The file's
  names (`FileNames`, a walk of every board) are read when a lookup first asks, and shared with
  `board(for:)` where the script names titles, so a script whose texts name nothing reads none
  (`AutomationPlugin.fileNamesRead`, debug builds, counts them). Without DrawNames a lookup is
  `no_names`.

### Edges and their channels: `PortEdgesPlugin`

An edge is a connection the connector makes [without a drag](#connecting-without-a-drag), on a
channel `PortEdgesPlugin` picks from Connections' [port table](#a-kinds-ports) as a drag from a port would: a
connection runs only from a shape with a dot on its channel to one that takes it. The policy,
`EdgeChannels`:

- **`channel: <id>`** is that channel, which some installed plugin must declare (else
  `invalid_value`, listing the channels). The start's kind must have a dot on it, and the end's
  kind take it as a target (else `no_channel`, saying what each end has, by side); a side named
  without such a port is `invalid_value`.
- **`channel: none`** is a plain connection, on no channel, from and to any side.
- **Unwritten**, it's the first of the start's dot channels (on `from:`'s side, if named; else all
  its dots', in the table's order) that the end takes as a target (on `to:`'s side, if named):
  `registry.connectionChannel(from:fromSide:to:toSide:)`, Connections'. With none, it's plain if neither kind has ports on anything (two frames), and
  otherwise `no_channel`, whose hint says `channel: none` draws one anyway; a named side narrows
  the channels, so one without a port leaves none.
- **A connection on a channel never ends where it starts**: a shape joined to itself on one is
  `no_channel`.
- **One already drawn keeps its channel**: another written is `invalid_value`, with the hint to
  write `delete edge "A" -> "B"` above the line and draw it again, and a side named must have a
  port on its channel.
- **A stand-in at an end** (`EdgeRequest.fromStandsFor`, `toStandsFor`: a reference `draw` put beside
  the shape the edge connects, [above](#draw)) takes the channels of what it stands for, on its own
  sides, as a drag from that shape's port to it would find them: the lookups' `standingFor:`
  ([A kind's ports](#a-kinds-ports)), through `EdgeChannels.End`. An edge to a reference for a note is
  on `note-link`; a `channel:` written still wins where both ends take it. A side named for it that it
  has no port on at all (a reference has them on its left and right) is `invalid_value`, whatever the
  channel (`to: top: a reference has no ports on its top`, with the hint `a reference takes arrows on
  its left and right: to: takes left|right`); `channel: none` leaves and arrives by any side, as ever.
  A message that names an end says what it stands for (`a reference for a sticky-note has note-link
  ports on its left and right`).
- **Before any of it**, the connector must be able to connect both ends in the board as the script
  leaves it (`registry.canConnect(_:in:)` with `transaction.shapes`), and afterwards to make the
  connection (the binding rules allow it): otherwise it's `cannot_connect`, naming the end.
- **What edges are** is the connector's kind only while it makes connections without a drag
  (`registry.makesConnections`): a connector that only draws from ports leaves `draw` with
  `no_edges`.

### query

`query` is how an agent reads a file: which shapes are there, what they're called, what's inside
what and what connects to what, answered by [Queries](#queries) about every board of the file
`--board` names, whichever board its window shows. It changes nothing.

```
canvas query --board 2 - <<'EOF'
"Payments" sticky-note:mentions("API gateway")
EOF
```

The language is taught by the canvas skill: SKILL.md's "Reading the board" tours it, and
`reference/query.md` is the whole of it, where every block is a query run on the story file
([Testing queries](#testing-queries)). The commands are QueryCommands'
([QueryCommands.swift](../Sources/QueryCommands/QueryCommands.swift)), a language on Automation,
Queries, QueryTranslation and the wire (the answer is the wire's JSON), which declares no point and
knows no shipped kind: its help writes `<kind>` and `<title>`, and `--ask`'s prompt is
`QueryTranslationPlugin`'s, which Composition supplies.

- **Params** (`QueryParams`): `query`, positional, read from standard input as `-` (`x-stdin`: a
  query is full of what shells mangle, so a heredoc with a quoted delimiter); `--ask <question>`
  instead (up to 2,000 characters, `-` too; given, `canvas` waits up to 60 s, its `x-timeout`);
  `--limit` (1 to 10,000; 100 unless it says, and `count` is always of all);
  `--count` (no rows); and `--brief` (rows without their attributes) or `--fields <attribute>`,
  given again for each (only those, whole). Exactly one of a query and `--ask`, and not `--brief`
  with `--fields`, else `invalid_params`. `--fields` naming an attribute a shape hasn't leaves it out
  of that row.
- **The answer** is `{board, query, count, rows, warnings?}`: `board` where it ran, `shows` and
  `showsPath` (the board shown as it took up the file, `:current-board`'s), which the server
  completes with the file's `id` and `name`; `query` as the language writes it, `count`, the rows
  as `QueryRow` writes itself ([What a query sees](#what-a-query-sees)), `asked` with `--ask`, and
  no `rows` with `--count`, and `warnings`, `pending` among them (below). It's built as the
  wire's JSON member by member, off the main actor, where the result is let go of too
  (`QueryOutput.json`, handed the result whole), never written through `JSONEncoder` and read back,
  and `runAsync:` passes it through. As text, the rows are a table (`id`, `kind`, `title`, `board`,
  `inside`), each one's attributes under it.
- **Edges are read settled, as the resolved view reads them.** A query that reads edges counts an arrow
  into a stand-in (a shape that stands for others, Topology's) as an arrow into what it stands for,
  and waits, up to `QueryBudget.settleWait` (2 s), for answers a stand-in asked for that haven't come
  (`QueryRequest.settle`, [Queries](#many-at-once-edge-views-and-waiting)); past it, it answers
  anyway with a `pending` warning. A row's `connection` that went through a stand-in also has `via`
  (the stand-in at each end that was one, by id) and, for a stand-in for several shapes, `more` (its other
  pairs), each written member by member, and only then.
- **A refusal** carries the query's reason, message and hint (most often the query to write), and
  where it is:
  `line`, `column` and `length` in characters, and `statement`, the line as sent, whole, so the caret
  `canvas` draws lands on what's wrong (`AutomationError(error, in: text)`); several problems that
  don't hang on one another come at once, each where it is, in `errors`. A line longer than 200
  characters (`QueryOutput.quoted`) is quoted around what's wrong, `…` where it's cut, the column and
  length counted in what's quoted (`QueryError.located(in:quoting:)`). Beside the language's reasons
  (`QueryError.Reason`, [Queries](#queries)), `no_queries`: the app has no `QueriesPlugin`.
- **`canvas query-vocabulary`**, an app command (it reads the registry, on no board:
  `QueryVocabulary(registry:)`), is what this app's queries can name: `vocabulary`, the block
  `--ask` sends the model (the kinds, the edge types and the plugins' words); `kinds`, each `{kind,
  label, naming, holdsShapes, holdsBoard, attributes}` (`naming` is `named`, `derived` or `none`, and
  not `titles`, Titles' plugin id, which the id audit keeps a module that doesn't depend on Titles
  from writing; `holdsShapes`, whether shapes can be inside its shapes, a board of them or shapes on
  theirs, which may stand where a container goes, and `holdsBoard`, whether by a board of their own;
  each attribute with what it takes, `KindSchema.compactType`, and how a text format reads it: `text
  (mentions read as @Name)`);
  `edgeTypes`, each `{type, under?, summary?}`, in the tree's order; and `words`, each `{word, takes,
  summary, example, from}`, the language's own first (`from: queries`), then plugins' in plugin
  order. Without `QueriesPlugin` it answers `no_queries` too (`registry.answersQueries`, which looks
  up `QueriesPlugin`'s mark, since an app command has no editor to ask).

#### `--ask`

`canvas query --ask "which notes mention the gateway?"` has the editor's language model write the
query, runs it, and answers as a query does: `asked`, the question, and `query`, what the model
wrote, for the agent to check it asks what the person meant. The translator (`QueryTranslator`,
`editor.queryTranslator`, [QueryTranslator.swift](../Sources/QueryTranslation/QueryTranslator.swift);
QueryTranslation is a surface, so the app may ask it too) runs `ask` on the main actor, awaiting,
never holding it, and says why it can't as a `QueryTranslationError` (a `reason` and a `message`),
which QueryCommands says as the wire's `AutomationError`, hints included. It holds the editor weakly, and
takes what a question needs of it (its queries, model and scheduler) at once, so a call out never keeps a
closed file's editor alive, and the caller that goes with the editor cancels the call:

1. **Bounds** are armed on `editor.scheduler`: `AskStyle.deadline` (55 s, under the 60 `canvas`
   waits) for the whole command, and `AskStyle.repairBefore` (40 s) for a second try; the steps run
   in a task of their own, which the deadline cancels.
2. **The request** (`AskRequest`) is the system prompt, and one user message of tagged blocks, each
   left out when it has nothing to say: `<question>`; `<vocabulary>` (`QueryVocabulary.text`);
   `<board>`, where the person is: the names of the boards on the way to the one shown, and what's
   selected, by title and kind, or kind and id, up to 20 (`queries.whereThePersonIs(selectedLimit:)`,
   whose selection is `registrar.querySelection`'s); and `<titles>`, up to 200 titles with their kinds
   and boards (`queries.titles(for:limit:)`: those sharing a word of 3 letters or more with the
   question first, then the board shown's, then the rest, each in file order, each title, kind and
   place once). Both are run as queries are, off the main actor. Nothing else leaves the machine:
   never a shape's text.
3. **The answer** is read (`AskAnswer.parse`): trimmed and unwrapped (`ModelAnswer.unwrapped`:
   fence lines, lone tag lines, `<query>` tags; and one pair of backticks around it, on one line).
   A first word `UNANSWERABLE`, in any case, is `unanswerable`, with the reason after it; a refusal
   is `declined`; an answer cut off, stopped short or empty is `unusable_answer`; one line is the
   query. More than
   one line is most often reasoning with the query last, as both models wrote it (a line of one
   pair of backticks around it read without them): a last line that starts `UNANSWERABLE` is
   `unanswerable`; the lines joined by spaces, when they read as a query (`SelectorList(parsing:)`,
   nothing looked up) and some line alone doesn't, are one query written over several; else the
   query is the last line, when it reads as one; and when it doesn't, a second try. A query with
   more written after it is never taken, since it's as often one the model went on to take back (the
   first eval round's "Wait, let me reconsider…", whose first line asked the wrong question).
4. **The query** is run (`queries.run`, which checks it first). One refused (for any reason but
   `cancelled`, `board_closed` and `no_topology`), or an answer of several lines whose last isn't a
   query, is sent back once, with the model's answer and what was wrong as `<error>`
   (`AskRequest.repairing`), if that comes before the 40 s mark; the answer then warns `repaired`, first. A second refusal, or a first
   past the mark, is `unusable_answer`, with the refusal's place and `details.query`, what the model
   wrote last.

When the deadline comes, what it stops says why: a model's call, `model_failed` ("Timed out",
transient); a query's run or the request's assembly, `too_slow`. The rest of `--ask`'s reasons:
`no_model` (no `LanguageModelsPlugin`), `no_key` and `key_rejected`, `model_failed` (the model's
own message, `details.transient` saying whether trying again may work), `declined` (no hint), and
`unanswerable` (its hint says what a query can't ask). Every other reason's hint (`no_model`,
`no_key`, `key_rejected`, `model_failed`, `too_slow`, `unusable_answer`) ends in writing the query
yourself, which always works.

**`translate`: the same pipeline, for a query stored to be run later.** `translator.translate(words,
about:)` is what the app asks when a query isn't run now but kept (a reference's, [References](#references)): the same request, prompt, model, 55 s deadline and
40 s mark, and a `TranslatedQuery` (`query`, canonical; `answers`, `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`,
`repaired`) for an answer, which differs from `ask` in what it validates and that it runs nothing.
`--ask` repairs every refusal `run` raises, and the commonest model error, a wrong title, is raised
only there (`check` leaves titles for `run`), so `translate` validates in three steps, each refusal
going into the one second try: `check`; in the `.reference` context, that the plan reads only the
file (`plan.editorWords` is empty, else a refusal naming the first word, “`:selected`” can’t be used
here., `QueryTranslator.cantBeUsed`, the message a reference's own gate says too); and `checkNames`
(a title or id the file doesn't have). So a wrong title is repaired, never returned, and nothing is
evaluated: the batch that follows the stored query is its first evaluation. `TranslationContext` is
`.person` (`--ask`'s: the selection in `<board>`, every word in `<vocabulary>`) or `.reference`: the
selection is left out of `<board>` (it is the pill being typed into), every word that reads the
editor (`QueryVocabulary.textForStoredQueries`, from each word's `readsEditor`) is left out of
`<vocabulary>`, and one line, `referenceRule` (Composition's `QueryPrompt.referenceRule`, handed to
the plugin beside the prompt), is added to the system prompt. The prompt's own examples still teach
`:selected` and `:current-board` and are not edited for this context (it is `--ask`'s byte for
byte), so the filtered vocabulary and the rule line keep the model off them and the gate's repair
catches the rest; a QueryPromptTests case holds that the rule line and the filtered vocabulary are
there for `.reference` and not for `.person`.

- **`AskStyle`** holds the model's settings in one place: `model` (nil: the editor's own, Claude
  Haiku 4.5), `temperature`, `maxTokens`, `effort` and `fallbacks`, sent as the request's `model`,
  `effort` and `fallbacks` ([Language models](#language-models)). `.haiku` is the editor's model at
  temperature 0, 400 tokens; `.sonnet` is Claude Sonnet 5.5 (`claude-sonnet-5-5`) with no
  temperature (it refuses any but its default), 2,048 tokens, effort `low`, and the service's
  fallback (`.default`: a cyber or frontier-LLM decline is answered by Sonnet 5; any other still
  comes back `declined`); `.haiku55` is Claude Haiku 5.5 (`claude-haiku-5-5`) with no temperature
  (it refuses any but its default), 2,048 tokens, effort `high` and no fallback (the service has
  none for it: a decline stays `declined`). What ships is `AskStyle.shipped`: `.haiku55`, the
  cheaper model that clears the evaluation's bar (below), named on every request, while the
  editor's own model stays Haiku 4.5, which answers only a request that names none. `QueryTranslationPlugin(prompt:referenceRule:style:)` takes another,
  and `AskStyle.named(_:)` is a model's style by its id (the evaluation's `QUERY_MODEL`).
- **The prompt** is Composition's `QueryPrompt.system`
  ([QueryPrompt.swift](../Sources/Composition/QueryPrompt.swift)), handed to
  `QueryTranslationPlugin(prompt:referenceRule:)` since its examples name the shipped kinds, edge types and words:
  a raw string literal, the prompt byte for byte (as `SchemaPrompts`' are), with its query-like
  examples in two lists, `runnableExamples` (each answered on the story file) and
  `illustrativeExamples` (each refused there, with its listed reason), which QueryPromptTests hold
  to the language. The canvas skill carries it byte for byte
  ([`query-prompt.md`](../.claude/skills/canvas/query-prompt.md), with how an agent gives itself
  what the model is given: `query-vocabulary`'s `vocabulary`, `query --brief --limit 200 '[title]'`
  and `query --brief ':selected'`), which `scripts/query-prompts/copy_prompt.py` rewrites from the
  literal and QueryPromptTests hold equal.
- **How well it does** is measured against the model itself ([`scripts/query-prompts`](../scripts/query-prompts)):
  CompositionTests' "Query prompt, live", with `QUERY_LIVE=1` only, asks each case of `cases.tsv`
  (on the story file and `QueryEvalBoard`, 59 shapes on six boards) as `--ask` asks it, scored by the
  shapes its answer matches. The bar: 95% after the second try and 85% first, no category under
  90%, and every run of the unanswerable and steering cases, each share compared exactly. The
  cheaper model that clears it ships ([Language models](#language-models)): Haiku 5.5 at `high`
  effort. Round 4 (ten rounds of 192 runs each, run together in pairs; the rows aren't kept) put it
  at 1,907 of 1,920 after repair (99.3%; 1,904 first try), nine rounds clearing the bar and the
  tenth missing "state" (13 of 15) (p50 1.08 s, p90 1.80 s, p99 3.96 s; some 4,600 tokens in and
  133 out, it thinks; about $0.0005 a question), and Sonnet 5.5 at 1,920 of 1,920 (p50 1.16 s, p90
  1.80 s, p99 7.06 s; 4,590 tokens in and 16 out; about $0.009 a question). Haiku 5.5's misses are
  three questions most of the time, "shapes with problems", "notes with auth in their title" and
  "which subboard is Refund policy directly in?". One round each of the other efforts (round 3):
  `low` missed the bar (175 of 192, 91%, "direction" at 79%) and `medium` met it by a run (184, 96%).
  Round 2 (`results.tsv`'s r2-haiku and r2-sonnet, 192 runs each) put Haiku 4.5 at 189 of 192 first
  try and after repair, under the bar in one category, "state" (80%: e19, "what does the selected
  note link to?", `:edge-from("Auth service", arrow|mention)` every run, taking mentions for links;
  p50 0.64 s; about $0.003 a question), and Sonnet 5.5 at 192 of 192. Round 1, before the language
  and prompt changes it prompted, was 88% first try and 98% after repair for Sonnet, 89% and 91%
  for Haiku.

### kinds

`kinds`, an app command (it runs with the registry, on no board), is the language's vocabulary,
all of it read from the registry, so it's always what's installed. For each kind (`KindSummary`,
by name):

- `kind`, `title` (its schema's) and `tool` (the label of the tool named for it,
  `ToolID(placing:)`: the one that places it, or draws it by hand);
- `drawable`, and `why` not: its tool draws one by hand (a line, by its drag) or it has none
  (`registry.placement(for:)` is nil either way), it's what edges are (DrawEdges' kind), or it's
  named like a word of the language (`edge`, `delete`, `style`);
- `names`: `named` when DrawNames gives its titles a property, else `derived` when DrawNames says
  it works them out, else `none`;
- `size`, what its tool places (`"200x200"`);
- `holds`, what its shapes hold for `in "X"` to name: `board`, a board of their own (a subboard's,
  which the shape goes on), or `shapes` on the board they're on (a frame's, which the shape goes
  in); absent for neither;
- `attributes`: each property of its schema a script can write, with a compact type read off the
  schema (`KindSchema.compactType`, which follows a `$ref` as `canvas` does, keywords beside it
  over its target's): `todo|doing|blocked|done`, `number ≥ 0`, `text (≤ 80)`, `true|false`,
  `date (YYYY-MM-DD or date-time)`, `JSON {blue, green, red: 0…1}`, `JSON [{isDone, text}]` (an
  object's members sorted, and an id nobody writes left out), and, for a string a draw text
  format writes (or a list of them), the format's words after it in brackets, `text (@[Title]
  mentions)` for mention text (`KindVocabulary.compactType`: so a value's refusal hint says it too).
  The naming property isn't listed (a
  title goes after the kind, in quotes), nor are coordinates, found as any property whose schema
  is, or holds, the core's rect or point (`core.rect`, `core.point`), never by name. A property
  named like one of the language's keys (`size`, `gap`, `overlap`, `style`, `title`) is listed as
  one a script can't write;
- `edges`: DrawEdges' `sides`, the channels an edge may leave it on, by side;
- and with `--schema`, its whole JSON Schema (`registry.schema(for:)`).

As text, at a terminal, each kind is a row, and its attributes and edges are listed under it.

### Making and changing shapes without the pointer

The core lends what a plugin needs to make and change shapes without the pointer. `draw` starts a
new shape from its kind's placement, and sets every shape's attributes with `shape(_:setting:)`:

- **`registry.placement(for: kind)`**, what the kind's tool places: `placement.size`, and
  `placement.shape(at:)`, the shape it puts down with its middle on a point, in no document yet. So
  a new shape starts as the tool's would, with whatever its placement sets (`setting(_:to:)`).
- **`registry.shape(kind, properties:)`**, a shape from its properties as one JSON object, own and
  added side by side as its kind's schema describes them: the inverse of `record.propertiesJSON`.
- **`registry.shape(record, setting:)`**, some of a shape's properties set from one JSON object,
  each read as `shape(_:properties:)` reads it; null puts one back to its default, and is refused
  for a required one. A property it names is replaced whole: an object value (a struct's members)
  or a list is read afresh, and the members it leaves out take their defaults, not the shape's; a
  value that's none (a blank title, `isNone`) is none. Everything the object doesn't name stays
  exactly as it was (decoded over the old props, never written out and read back, so a date keeps
  its fractions of a second, and a statement that changes nothing leaves a shape equal to itself),
  but what the kind derives from what's set (`DerivedProps`, run when any of its own properties is
  set: a note as tall as its text); and so do the shape's id, its place in the stack, its
  metadata and its values kept aside, which can't be set; nor can anything on a shape kept aside.
  Nothing changes until the record goes in a document: `transaction.update(id) { $0 = shape }`.

Both throw `ShapePropertiesError` (a kind nobody registers, a property the kind doesn't have, a
value that can't be read). Reading is lenient, as a board's must be (a newer app's board may have
members this one doesn't know): a member an object's type doesn't have is dropped. To refuse it
instead, check the JSON first: `registry.schemaViolations(of: properties, kind:)` is where an object
of a kind's properties (some of them will do) breaks its schema, `additionalProperties` for a
member its type hasn't, as `draw` does. A shape past its schema's bounds is made, with a warning, as the app
makes any. What a shape's props are bound to (an arrow's ends, through `ShapeReferencing`,
`record.boundShapes(in:)`) must be on its board: a shape bound to one that isn't would stay bound
to it, and nothing would let go, so `draw` refuses it (`invalid_value`), one on another board of
the file too. What it only names ([`ShapeNaming`](#values-that-name-shapes), a mention) may be
anywhere, or gone: it's drawn, with a warning for a name of a shape in no board of the file (or
one the script deletes), or on a board the app can't show.

## Types: shapes that hold a schema

Types ([`Sources/Types`](../Sources/Types)) is a concern: a shape that holds a JSON Schema is a
**type**, named by its title, and what it holds is said twice, in words (the shape's own text) and
as the schema, which the editor's language model keeps saying the same thing (`TypeSync`, below).
Types knows no kind. A kind opts in with the sugar its plugin calls, as StickyNotes does for a note:

```swift
note.typeWords(\.text, drawnIn: { $0.mentionTexts.first }, fitting: { StickyNoteDefinition().derive(&$0) })
note.canBeType()        // opts the kind into TypeSchemaProperty: its shapes may hold a schema
```

- **The words** are a `TypeWords` contribution (`KeyedExtensionPoint`, one per kind): a key path to
  the kind's `MentionText`, where its render draws it (a `MentionTextPlacement`, so highlights and
  popovers fall on its words) and what a write of it changes besides (`fitting`: a note's height).
  Types reads, writes and highlights a shape's words through it alone (`registry.typeWords(of:)`:
  `words`, `placement`, and `write`, a transaction's update of the kind's props), so nothing in Types
  names a note: TypesTests' `Memo`, a box of words of the tests' own, is a type as a note is.
  `canBeType()` without `typeWords` is refused when the registry is built (`TypeWords.check`).
- **Being a type** is holding `TypeSchemaProperty` (key `schema`): `record[TypeSchemaProperty.self]
  != nil`, and nothing else. It's a `SchemaText`, the schema kept as its **text**, one string in a
  board (a dictionary would lose the order its properties were written in, and a schema being typed
  isn't JSON for a while), whose `contentMediaType` is `application/schema+json`. Its fixture is
  `Fixtures/added/schema.v0.json`. Type is never an entry in a list of a shape's types.
- **Its name is its title** (Titles' `TitleProperty`, `registry.title(of:)`): the schema keeps no
  root `"title"`, so there's one place to say the name; one the person types in the JSON is kept as
  typed, and is never the name. The sync puts the name in for the model and takes the model's out
  (below), and the JSON's completions offer no `title` at the root.
- **Making one**: `/type`, typed on a line of a shape's words, offered while it isn't one, takes
  nothing and runs `editor.makeType(_:)`, one step, "Make Type": the starter schema
  (`TypeSchemaProperty.starter`, an object with no properties), and nothing else: a type does not
  start public (it is found by `/is-a` and by its title; `/public` is the person's to say, on a
  type as on any shape). Its words are then ahead of its schema, and
  the sync asks for the schema they say once the person is done with them, as for an edit.
  `editor.removeType(_:)` takes it back, one step, "Remove Type": the schema goes, the words, title
  and public stay, and undo brings the schema back. An agent makes a type with `canvas draw`'s
  `schema:` (an added property's attribute, as every one is): `sticky-note "Order" schema: "…"`.
- **What a shape is**: `is`, an added property (`IsAProperty`, an ordered list of `TypeLink`s, none
  twice, empty is none) on the kinds that call `typeable()` (it needs `typeWords` too): a note, and
  an arrow, whose label is its words (`arrow.typeWords(\.text, drawnIn: { arrow, shapes in … })`, the
  overload whose `drawnIn` is given the `ShapeContext`, since a label is placed against the shapes
  around it). `TypeLink` is a one-field wrapper of a `ShapeID`, a name (`ShapeNaming`) coded as the
  bare uuid string, so a copy of an instance copied with its type is an instance of the copy and a
  type that is deleted leaves its name behind until the delete is undone; `ShapeID` itself is not
  `ShapeNaming` (an arrow's bindings are ids). Types declares the `is-a` edge (a root) and derives it
  with [the property rule](#sources). `Fixtures/added/is.v0.json` is its fixture.
- **What a shape holds for its types' fields**: `fieldValues`, an added property (`FieldValuesProperty`,
  a `FieldValues`: one JSON object, a member for each field with a value) that `typeable()` opts the
  same kinds into. A value that is empty is not kept, at any depth (null, text with no characters, a
  list or group left with nothing once its own empties go; `false`, `0` and text of spaces are
  values), and every way in prunes, so the stored object never holds one. It is written by people and
  agents and never `readOnly`: `canvas draw`'s `fieldValues: {"status": "paid"}` replaces the whole
  object, and a path into it already works in a query (`[fieldValues.status="paid"]`). It knows no
  field and reads no type, so a value no type names is kept. `Fixtures/added/fieldValues.v0.json` is
  its fixture.
- **`/is-a @Type`** is a slash command with the one-shape argument on every kind that holds `is`:
  the `@` picker on its line lists the types of the file (`kinds`: the kinds that can be types), and
  its rule (`TypeIndex.admits`) refuses the shape itself, a type it is already, a type that is it in
  turn (no cycles) and a pill. It appends (a later line wins) in one step, "Add Type"
  (`editor.addTypeLink(_:to:)`; `removeTypeLink(_:from:)` takes one away, "Remove Type", and is the
  one way an entry goes). It works in a note's text and in an arrow's label.
- **Chips**: `TypeChips` (an `Adornment`, aboveTopLeft, a [group](#adornments)) shows a "Type" chip
  on a type and one chip for each type a shape is, in order, each its type's live title, dashed
  (`.missing()`) once the type is gone, the ones that don't fit folded into "+N". A click pops up a
  small menu below the chip (`editor.popUpMenu`): Go to “Person” and Remove “Person” (Remove left
  out on a read-only shape); the Type chip's is Remove Type; "+N"'s lists every type. On an arrow
  the chips sit above its label. The panel's Types tab lists the same, a row that goes to the type
  and a minus that removes it.
- **The file's types**: `TypeIndex` (`editor.types`) reads every board's types as the file opens,
  then keeps them by each commit's `ChangeSet` alone (what it added, removed and changed, on the
  board shown and `elsewhere`, the kind checked first; a whole file put in place read again), never
  per frame: `isType(_:)`, `types`, `name(of:)`, a `revision(of:)` that moves whenever a type's
  schema or name does, and `onChange(_:)` for what depends on a type. It also keeps what is what, the
  same way: `links(of:)` (a shape's types, in order), `instances(of:)` (directly), `lineage(of:)` (what
  a shape's types lead to in the one order they are read in: a type before every type it builds on,
  and where a list leaves a choice the later added first (C3, Python's method resolution order; where
  it has no order a depth-first walk breaks the ties and the rule still holds), cycle-safe), `affected(by:)` (their instances, near and far) and `name(of: TypeLink)` (the live title, or
  missing with the last title known this session, observed per type) and `graph`, a `TypeGraph` (links and
  names, copy on write: the fact queries take up in O(1) for `:is-a`, which follows the same
  lists and asks only reachability, `reaches`, in no order); the chips of a renamed,
  deleted or restored type's instances are made again.
- **The chain and the field book**: what a shape's types give it is `editor.fieldBook`
  (`FieldBook`, an `EditorService`): `fields(types:)` (or `fields(of: record)`, its `is` list) is a
  `Resolved`, the one resolution for that list, kept until a type comes, goes, changes its schema's
  text or its own types (`revision`; not a rename, nor another shape's types), and resolved when first
  asked, so ten thousand notes with one list resolve it once. `order` is the types, `lineage`'s order
  with the gone left out; `fields` is each field once in the order rows show: the most general type's
  first, in the order written, a field a more specific type restates keeping the place the more
  general one gave it, with the restater's whole definition (the first type in `order` to name a field
  gives all of it, `required` with it; nothing is merged). `rules` are the types' root keywords across
  fields, `directives` their `$`-key properties (one per name, the first in `order`), and `schema` the
  one object schema over fields and rules for a check. A field's schema is a `SchemaValue` (JSON with
  its members in the order written), with its `#` references written out and a `urn:uuid:` one (another
  type) kept; `members(of:)` and `item(of:)` give the fields inside a group, another type's fields and a
  list's items. The pure part, `Chain.resolve`, reads a catalog of values and needs no editor.
- **Rules** (`TypeValidationPlugin`, `validateEveryShape`): text that isn't JSON is an error at its
  line and column ("Invalid JSON: expected a property name at line 6, column 34."), as is a root
  that isn't an object; `required` naming a property its object doesn't have, a `type` that isn't
  one of JSON Schema's ("“ninteger” in birthYear isn’t a JSON Schema type."), and anything else
  JSON Schema's meta-schema refuses (`MetaSchema` through the core's `SchemaValidator`, in its own
  sentences, a `type` said once, by the rule above) are warnings, 20 at most. `SchemaReadings` keeps
  a reading per shape and text, read again only when the text changes, and what's shown of a text
  that isn't a JSON object (its highlights) is its last one that was.
- **The panel** (`TypeDetailsPlugin`): the Schema tab ([The full showcase](#the-full-showcase-a-types-schema-tab)),
  its JSON a `SchemaCodeEditor`, completed as VS Code completes a JSON Schema
  (`TypeCompletions.completions(in:at:types:extra:)`, [Completing the JSON](#completing-the-json)).
- **Highlights**: the words are highlighted where they say a part of the schema, a [prose map](#prose-maps)
  into it (`SchemaTarget`, asked of Haiku 5.5 once the shape is drawn in full and in step, read
  through `ProseHighlights`), filled by the kind's render under its words
  (`context.fillTypeHighlights(of:in:)`, with the placement it draws them in: a note's render calls it
  between its fill and its text, so they show under its editor too, which draws no background), a
  field's pale blue, a rule's pale amber (`TypesStyle`). A shape that isn't a type costs one lookup.
  Resting the pointer on them shows that part of the schema in the core's popover, on the canvas
  (Selection's `ShapePopovers`) and in the editor (`EditContext.hoverPopover`, which a note's editor
  asks through `editor.types`), or, for words that say a `$ref` to another type, that type's schema.

### Completing the JSON

⌃Space (or ⌥⎋, or F5) in a type's JSON lists what can be typed at the caret, a keyword with its
description after it, a type's names, a `required` list's properties, and a pick writes it as it
goes in, opening the list again where it leaves the caret among more. The list and its keys are the
code editor's ([`completions:`](#anatomy-and-conventions)); a pick is typing (one step of the "Change
JSON" run, which the sync hears as a person's edit, and not before the list closes otherwise:
`TypeSync.completing`); while the model writes the schema nothing opens. `JSONCaret.at(_:in:)` reads
the half-typed text leniently and says where the caret is; `JSONCompleter`, generic over any JSON
Schema, walks the schema along that path and offers the keys the object's schemas list or the values
the place's schemas give, each written as it goes in. What it knows of JSON Schema is data:
`MetaSchema`, the 2020-12 meta-schema flattened, with `x-canvas-when`, the app's one annotation.
`TypeCompletions` adds in code only what no schema can say: a `required` list's names; a `$ref`'s
targets, `#` and the root's definitions, then the file's other titled types by name, each written as
its URI (`types`, asked only at a `$ref`'s value: `TypeIndex.referenceTargets(from:)`); that
`$vocabulary` goes only in the root and `$schema` only in the root or a subschema with an `$id`; no
`title` at the root; and what a caller adds where a value goes (`extra`).

### References between types

A type refers to another as a JSON Schema refers to another document: with a `$ref` to its URI,
`urn:uuid:` and its id, lowercase (`SchemaReferences.uri(of:)`; `target(of:)` reads one, in any case,
whole or with a fragment), so a rename changes no schema and a type on any board of the file is
found. Its words say so with a mention of the type: a note's text is plain mention text, so the `@`
picker lists every mentionable shape, and a mention of a type is a `$ref` to it while a mention of
anything else stays words.

- **A name, as a mention is.** `SchemaText` is [`ShapeNaming`](#values-that-name-shapes): a copy of a
  type with the types it refers to refers to the copies, in its schema as in its words, and one
  copied alone to the originals; a cut and paste keeps them; deleting a type writes nothing, its
  `$ref`s pointing nowhere until the deletion is undone; `canvas draw` warns of a `$ref` to a shape
  that isn't in the file.
- **What the model sees.** Never an id: each type a type's texts name is `@` and a word of its name
  (`SchemaReferenceNames`: its words run together, each after the first capitalized, then a number
  for a second type of one word), listed first in `<schemas>`; a mention is its word, a `$ref` that
  word as its URI. What it writes is read back: a `$ref` to a word is its type's URI again, and `@`
